headline: High-risk default interaction: ECC can write shared files and use MCP while Kestra can execute broad external actions, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write filesystem and use MCP, and Kestra can read/write files and consume stdin/stdout. A shared workspace or copied outputs could let ECC content be treated as instructions by Kestra. The pairwise pathway is plausible in default tooling, though not directly documented, so uncertainty stays at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF ECC outputs are copied into Kestra task definitions or scripts without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a writable workspace or storage path, attacker-controlled content can bridge them.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Disable automatic ingestion of agent-generated text into Kestra tasks.
Add a manual review step before Kestra executes any ECC-produced artifact.
Use provenance labels on files passed between agents.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing for inter-agent handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, git history, security findings, and files under ~/.claude; Kestra touches logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, database data, and cloud storage data. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive material can flow from ECC into Kestra outputs or external systems. The profiles show enough overlap to make leakage plausible in default setups.
conditions: IF ECC session files or git history contain secrets and are mounted into Kestra storage, leakage occurs.
IF Kestra tasks export artifacts or notifications containing ECC-managed data, sensitive context can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Keep ECC and Kestra on separate volumes.
Restrict Kestra access to only the files it needs.
Rotate any shared credentials before pairing.
Review logs and artifacts for sensitive fields.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret scoping and redaction.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write filesystems. ECC also modifies git state, while Kestra can drive Docker/Kubernetes/SSH and has root/docker.sock requested. Concurrent writes to shared paths or repositories can corrupt state or overwrite each other, and the blast radius can be irreversible. This is a default-dangerous overlap.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory without locking, write conflicts can corrupt state.
IF Kestra tasks invoke Docker or SSH against resources ECC also edits, concurrent mutation can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories and repos.
Serialize writes with a lock file or queue.
Disable git mutation in one agent during shared runs.
Run one agent read-only when the other is active.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking and resource arbitration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces security findings, documentation, and agent outputs, while Kestra is an automation/orchestration system with email, Slack, PagerDuty, cloud, and database actions. If Kestra treats ECC output as authoritative, a mistaken or injected result can trigger downstream actions at scale. The pair creates a strong A-to-B automation chain with irreversible consequences.
conditions: IF Kestra workflows consume ECC-generated findings or commands without verification, downstream actions can be wrong.
IF ECC output is routed into notification or deployment tasks, a single bad result can fan out broadly.
mitigations: Require human approval before Kestra acts on ECC output.
Add schema validation for all ECC-to-Kestra handoffs.
Limit Kestra to dry-run mode for paired workflows.
Tag ECC outputs as untrusted by default.
requires-engineering: implement verification gates and rollback for automated actions.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles security findings, session data, and git history; Kestra handles logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, and cloud/database data. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, but the data classes and broad external APIs make retention and residency mismatch plausible. Because uncertainty must escalate, medium is safer than low.
conditions: IF ECC-managed data includes regulated records and Kestra stores them in logs or artifacts, retention mismatch occurs.
IF Kestra routes EU-origin data to cloud services without a DPA or residency controls, compliance exposure occurs.
mitigations: Classify data before passing it between agents.
Disable logging of sensitive fields in Kestra.
Confirm residency and retention settings for both systems.
Keep regulated data out of shared workflows.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
